articles.title: Kevin Blake's Ebor Festival tips: Sky Sports Racing expert looks ahead to York's opening day with three selections
articles.summary: Day one of the York Ebor Festival takes place on Wednesday and is headlined by the Juddmonte International Stakes; Sky Sports Racing's Kevin Blake has put up three selections on the undercard on the Knavesmire
articles.body:
The Ebor Festival at York can make a game claim to be one of the very best four days of Flat racing anywhere in Europe. It is packed with quality stakes races and fiercely-competitive handicaps that present a great challenge no matter what your preferences. I'll do my best to pull a few winners from it in the coming days in this column....

The opening Hong Kong Jockey Club World Pool Handicap (1:50) starts this meeting off on Wednesday in devilishly-difficult style. Cases can be made across the track and while he has shortened up in price since the betting opened, I am sticking with the Richard Spencer-trained The Man .

Spencer is on track to have his best-ever year, and he is particularly good in these valuable sprint handicaps. The Man has shown a liking for this track, winning here in May 2025 and finishing an excellent head second in this race off 92 last year.

A winter in Dubai didn't yield the riches it promised, but it would be no surprise at all if his connections have been targeting this meeting with him ever since he returned from his post-Dubai break. He has had two runs to blow away the cobwebs in the last seven weeks and shaped well on both occasions. He can be expected to be at fever pitch here and with the draw appealing as having been kind to him, a big effort should be forthcoming.

The Tattersalls Acomb Stakes (2:25) is the first of what will be a feast of two-year-old races at this meeting, and my preference is for the Ed Walker-trained Alfred Wallace . A son of Dubawi out of the wonderful race mare Snow Lantern, he is certainly bred to be smart. He showed plenty of promise when putting up a good figure in victory at Thirsk in May and shaped well for a long way before weakening late after forcing the pace in the Superlative Stakes at Newmarket.

Switched to an even stiffer seven furlongs in the Pat Eddery Stakes at Ascot, his connections opted to experiment with completely different tactics by dropping him in and riding with patience. The experiment proved to be a roaring success, as he overcame trouble in running to produce a fine winning effort. He could well be able to improve on that now that the key to him has been found and I expect him to run a big race.

My final selection of the day comes in another ridiculously competitive sprint handicap, the Irish Thoroughbred Marketing Handicap (4:45). It is worth taking a shot on the Michael Keady-trained Underwriter . The three-year-old might well prove to be one of the bargains of the season, as he was bought by current connections for just 4,600gns in a Tattersalls online sale at the beginning of July.

His first run for them only showed subtle promise, but his latest effort in a valuable sprint handicap at Ascot was notably eye-catching. Locked up and shuffled back to last in his group inside the final furlong, he flashed home in the final 100 yards and would have been third in another stride. That was very promising indeed and with the handicapper having dropped him quite aggressively from his high of 92, he looks a well-handicapped horse. If he can build on his Ascot effort, he will have a very serious chance.

articles.title: Hollie Doyle blog: Constitution River can come of age in Juddmonte International showdown with Ombudsman
articles.summary: Ombudsman and Constitution River set to do battle in thrilling Juddmonte International on day one of York's Ebor Festival; Doyle cheering on husband Tom Marquand aboard Maltese Cross in the Sky Bet Great Voltigeur Stakes
articles.body:
Aidan set for 8th success in mouthwatering Juddmonte

The remarkably versatile Ombudsman will be tough to deny in the £1.5m Juddmonte International Stakes (3.35), a stunning highlight on day one of the Ebor Festival at York on Wednesday.

John and Thady Gosden's five-year-old has added the Group 1 Dubai Turf in Meydan and the Prince of Wales' Stakes at Royal Ascot to his illustrious CV since taking this race in such spectacular style 12 months ago.

However, Aidan O'Brien's CONSTITUTION RIVER is something very special as he proved in the French Derby and the Coral-Eclipse and can come of age against his older rival in what promises to be an epic duel.

Two years younger and benefiting from that 7lb allowance, the son of Wootton Bassett hasn't yet reached his peak and is adaptable enough to lower the colours of Godolphin's superstar in what looks certain to be another tactical renewal.

Juddmonte's representative Item has proven his liking for this track with wins at Group 2 level in the Dante and the York Stakes but despite being only 2lb behind Constitution River on official ratings, needs to dig much deeper to usurp the main two.

MALTESE CROSS can stake his claim for the 250th running of the St Leger with a big performance in the Sky Bet Great Voltigeur Stakes (3.00) at York - a traditional trial for next month's final Classic.

My husband Tom (Marquand) is rightfully hopeful he can avenge his Derby defeat by Christmas Day in this 1m4f Group 2 after a hard-fought success in the Group 1 Grand Prix de Paris last month.

He'd have been an unlucky loser that day after overcoming all sorts of problems in running and should enjoy this galloping test on a sound surface on The Knavesmire before stepping up in trip at Doncaster.

Christmas Day couldn't repeat his Epsom heroics in the Irish Derby when his stablemate Pierre Bonnard finished only a neck behind him. In fact, I wouldn't be surprised to see that lovely colt emerge as the main Ballydoyle threat to Maltese Cross.

HAFFNER is the one they all have to beat in the Group 3 Tattersalls Acomb Stakes (2.25) at York despite finding one too good in the Vintage Stakes at Goodwood.

Aidan O'Brien's colt, who had previously won a Newmarket maiden, emerged with plenty of credit behind the unbeaten Dr Rascal on the Downs and has much less to prove than his rivals over this 7f.

If he under-performs, Ed Walker's talented colt Alfred Wallace could be the one to take advantage. The son of top-class race mare Snow Lantern gained a deserved success in a Listed contest at Ascot last time and can find the necessary improvement to go well in this better grade.

Madera can avenge unlucky run in Stewards' Cup

The big sprint handicaps at York are notoriously difficult to solve but I can make a strong case for TOCA MADERA in the opening Hong Kong Jockey Club World Pool Handicap (1.50).

David O'Meara's gelding would have gone much closer in the Stewards' Cup at Goodwood with a clear run and has been given the chance to gain compensation off an unchanged mark with stable jockey Danny Tudhope back on board.

I'm pleased to see him drawn low in stall four as I think that's the best place to be on the straight track, which we know plays to the strengths of the well supported The Man . Richard Spencer's runner was second in this last year but was well behind Toca Madera at Goodwood last month.

A better alternative at a bigger price may be Lemos de Souza's gelding Naana's Sparkle who finished in front of them both in that Goodwood sprint and will hopefully get a good tow into the race from his middle draw at rewarding odds.

I nominated SMALL FRY as my 'Hot Shot' in this blog after his luckless run at the Goodwood Festival so won't be forsaking him in the Sky Bet Stayers Handicap (4.10) at York.

Joseph O'Brien's gelding got shuffled back at an important stage of the valuable Summer Handicap but still powered home to be a close second over 1m6f and can gain compensation despite a 4lb rise.

The step up to 2m can only be a positive for Joseph's son of Harzand who stays well and for the first time has the assistance of Ireland's champion jockey Dylan Browne McMonagle.

Andrew Balding's Shrimp Shady is becoming quite a force in top staying handicaps so don't rule him out either. He was second at the Shergar Cup after landing a big pot at Newbury at the expense of the likeable Team Player and will enjoy the test ahead of him on The Knavesmire.

articles.title: Formula 1: Kimi Antonelli - the boy 'born in a garage' and made on the track
articles.summary: Kimi Antonelli was a natural driver at the age of three, according to his dad. Here's how he went on to lead the F1 drivers' championship at the age of 19.
articles.body:
Kimi Antonelli was 10 when his father Marco first realised the boy sitting on his lap, operating the steering and gears, might have an exceptional talent as a racing driver.

The pair were at the Adria circuit in north-east Italy, Marco with his Lamborghini sports car team, Kimi competing in a karting race.

It was the end of the day and Marco, a former driver himself, asked his son: "Do you want to try the Lamborghini?"

Marco strapped himself and Kimi into the car, belts extended around both. Dad was in charge of the throttle and brake, his son would control the rest.

"I couldn't see the track because he was in front of me with a helmet on," Marco tells BBC Sport. "I could only see beside me the marker panels before each corner - 100m, 50m.

"We started to drive, step by step, faster, faster, faster. In the end, I pushed like I was alone and I arrived at the braking point at the end of the straight, 320km/h, braked very hard and at the limit.

"The car had a lot of oversteer. Kimi controlled the oversteer perfectly, then I went on the throttle, Kimi finished the oversteer, changed gear, and went.

"I said: 'OK, stop, because it has now become dangerous.' But when I saw the video, 10 years old, on my leg, oversteer, everything perfect, I said: 'Maybe he has something special.'"

Now a 19-year-old Kimi is dominating this year's F1 championship in only his second season.

This is the story of a boy his dad says was "born in a garage".

"Kimi from 15 days old was in the garage and heard the sound of the engine and the smell of the exhaust," says Marco, who worked with his wife Veronica on their racing team business.

It was the Christmas holidays when Kimi was about three, and Marco had brought home a simulator he had bought for his guests to try out at the Bologna Motor Show.

"Each evening, Kimi wanted to drive," Marco remembers.

Just like seven years later in the Lamborghini, Kimi would sit on Marco's leg, the controls divided in the same way.

"I remember one night I started to fall asleep because I had been at work very early and we had a crash because I didn't brake when we arrived at the end of the straight," Marco says.

"And Kimi said: 'Dad, dad, no sleep, no sleep. I have to drive.'"

Marco Antonelli did not originally want his son to become a racing driver, because of his own struggles during his career.

"Sometimes you are fast but not in the right position to become a professional driver," he says.

In the 1990s, Marco Antonelli was on the cusp of becoming a works driver in the DTM touring car series, then a huge hit with audiences across Europe.

He tested for Alfa Romeo, but then the team boss left and the opportunity evaporated. Another chance came up with BMW, alongside Roberto Ravaglia and Steve Soper - stars at the time. Again, the same thing happened.

"I suffered a lot for it," Marco says. "And, of course, I was scared that my son [would] relive the same situation. At the beginning, I was very stressed about the passion my son had for motorsport."

Kimi tried a go-kart for the first time when he was five, and immediately showed an awareness of racing lines, braking points and car control.

The Antonellis were what Marco describes as "a normal family". They could not possibly afford to pay for Kimi to take part in all the categories on the way to Formula 1.

Marco decided he could fund Kimi through karting and a year of the basic single-seater category, Formula 4. After that, he figured he might be able to put him in one of his GT cars and become professional that way.

But Kimi immediately started to impress. Whatever category he got into, he was quick, and won.

By the time Kimi was 11, his name was buzzing around motor racing circles. Mercedes heard about him, and their driver academy scout Gwen Lagrue flew to Italy to check him out.

It was a season in which Antonelli had ended up driving a kart with less power than those of his rivals. Marco had told Kimi this would be good for him - he should think not about the result, but about how to improve, always push hard.

"Gwen was impressed about this condition of power and driving in this category that Kimi did," Marco says. "And maybe they understood that Kimi was a different child."

Now Kimi was a member of the Mercedes driver academy, Marco could stop worrying about money, and start focusing on helping his son achieve his full potential.

Mercedes were not the only big names in F1 who had noticed Antonelli's promise.

"When he was in karting, you could already see he was one of the stand-out talents," says four-time world champion Max Verstappen, the only other teenager to win an F1 race.

At 15, Antonelli was ready to move up to cars, and, as a final preparation, did a couple of races in a karting category with gears. On his debut, with minimal pre-event testing, he took pole position. After that, he went to the world final, and stuck it on pole again.

This was the end of 2021, after which Antonelli moved full-time into cars. Through 2022, he swept the board in various championships in Formula 4, and the same happened in Formula Regional in 2023.

By now, Mercedes team boss Toto Wolff was already thinking that Antonelli would be his next F1 driver, potentially a replacement for Lewis Hamilton. With the seven-time champion approaching 40, Wolff was planning on taking control of that generational transition.

So when it came time to negotiate a new contract with Hamilton in 2023, Wolff played hardball. Hamilton wanted to sign for at least two firm years, Wolff only one. In the end, they compromised on a contract for 2024 with an option for 2025.

Hamilton, unimpressed, decided to look at his options, and signed to join Ferrari in 2025, telling Wolff in late January 2024, before the start of that season.

Wolff immediately phoned Marco Antonelli, to tell him the "very big news".

"'We put Kimi in Formula 1,'" Marco remembers Wolff saying. "'What do you think?'

"I said: 'Oh, [it] is a difficult question you ask me. Of course I'm happy that you think about Kimi but are you sure he's ready?'"

Mercedes were at a management away day. Wolff called his senior engineers together to tell them about Hamilton's decision.

"We were reviewing options and trying to come to a fairly rapid conclusion," says trackside engineering director Andrew Shovlin.

"We were all keen to just go with Kimi, which we knew was a bit of a risk. But it was quite exciting and we thought, based on his career to date, he had a good chance of being very good. It seemed like a good challenge."

Antonelli had not even driven an F1 car when Wolff made the call. Mercedes put together a testing programme for him, 20-odd days in cars a couple of years old at tracks all over the world to prepare him for his F1 debut in 2025.

Shovlin and the engineers were immediately impressed.

"It was how rapidly he would get up to speed," Shovlin says. "What you normally see with drivers is they're just incrementally going a little bit quicker, braking a bit later.

"If you compare with other drivers we've seen in an F1 car for the first time, the best I'd ever seen until then was George [Russell]. You suddenly saw someone who was quite similar.

"With Kimi, he took a couple of runs to work out how the car behaved and then he'd be more or less on the limit.

"The other thing you can see is the fidelity of the car control, how they can sit with it right on the edge of breaking away from them on entry to a corner, but they can just control it in that condition.

"Equally, when you looked at the mistakes he was making, they were often errors of judgement or lack of experience. They weren't run-out-of-talent mistakes."

Antonelli made one of these at the 2024 Italian Grand Prix. Wolff decided to give him his first experience of an F1 weekend in first practice at his home race at Monza.

It was a spectacular debut - for both good and bad reasons.

Antonelli set the fastest time on his first lap. Then he went for another. He was flying, miles quicker than anyone up to that point, but then he crashed heavily at the final corner, Parabolica.

"No-one on earth could have got the car around the corner at the speed he was attempting," Shovlin says. "He clearly got into his head that he would try and do something special and it was an error of judgment."

Wolff took Antonelli aside, told him it was OK, and not to worry about it. But the crash had a significant impact on Antonelli.

Wolff was very clear in public about managing expectations of Antonelli going into his debut season.

"I conditioned myself so strong that I said: 'There's going to be moments of brilliance and moments where you want to tear your hair out'," Wolff says.

There were stand-out moments, including pole for the sprint in Miami.

But the middle part of the season, through Europe, was a disappointment. A change to the rear suspension design made the car nervous and rocked his confidence. His pace was not impressive, and he made too many mistakes.

"We expected more highlights from him," Shovlin says.

Marco Antonelli explains: "Mercedes needed to have a good result after a period that was not like the Hamilton era. And, of course, needed two cars that always take points.

"Kimi felt this necessity. The crash in Monza was very tough for him to forget. It created on him a big pressure."

Wolff said the "moments of brilliance were there" but then there was "a spell of nine races that was really not good".

"Me, personally, I never doubted," says Wolff. "Other people doubted. In the team and externally."

A year on from his practice debut, Antonelli crashed again in Monza practice.

"This was the point where I said: 'Kimi, you've got to turn this around. This is just not good enough'," says Wolff. "He said: 'I know.'"

Marco Antonelli says he and his son talked a lot during this period and that Kimi "understood that everything can change".

"The period was bad but you can see light at the end of the tunnel," he says. "And step by step he started to take confidence."

Once F1 had left Europe in the autumn of last year, there was a shift.

"Suddenly, we felt like we were making really good progress," says Shovlin.

"There were signs towards the end of the year. I'm not saying any of us thought we'd see what we've seen so far this year, but that we had a decent F1 driver."

Antonelli has been rather more than that this year. He has taken the season by storm, and established a consistent supremacy over Russell.

In the best car in the field, Antonelli has taken six poles and six wins in 11 races and heads into the second half of the season, starting at the Dutch Grand Prix this weekend, with a 50-point lead in the championship, and well on course for his first world title. If it had not been for dodgy reliability, he could be even further ahead.

The extent of this turnaround has shocked almost everyone.

"We were all surprised," Wolff says. "My thoughts were always that he needed to make the experience of knowing all the tracks, the pressure of performing on such a high level under the spotlight of the media, the constant public feedback, whether you're doing well or not, the situations everyone wanted to be close to him.

"There wasn't one single defining factor where I would have said that made it difficult for him, but this year, he knew exactly what to expect. What was really nice to see is that the self-confidence, without feeling any entitlement, has shone."

Marco points to his son's "very strong" mentality.

"In F4 and Freca, he started with not good results, and he was able to remake everything and, at the end, work hard and win the championship," he says.

"We talk about F1. I don't know what the spark is in his brain, but Kimi in the past did the same."

Verstappen says: "For me, there was never any doubt that he would make the jump the year after and already be a lot more consistently competitive.

"It's normal in the progression of a driver. In your rookie season, it can be quite tough, but at the moment, of course, he's doing an amazing job."

Kimi pays tribute to his father, describing him as his "rock", while Wolff also praises the driver's "typical Italian family".

"They are caring, they are loving," Wolff says. "Kimi's character, he's gentle, he has empathy, he has charisma, he has the right amount of intelligence for being a racing driver."

Antonelli-Russell contrast could hardly be more stark Published 7 June

Antonelli-Russell contrast could hardly be more stark

Antonelli says he still has questions to answer Published 11 June

Antonelli says he still has questions to answer

Mercedes have been talking to Antonelli about managing his emotions, which have flared at times this season, such as in the sprint in Canada, when the racing between the two Mercedes drivers came close to boiling over.

Shovlin says: "He just says: 'I'm young, I'm Italian, what do you expect?'"

The remark reveals Antonelli's sense of humour, but also a maturity and self-awareness that might not always be expected in someone so young.

Wolff says: "He has all that. He's actually not [fitting the stereotype of] a typical emotional Italian. He's so clear [in] what he needs to do in a car. I don't see lots of emotion. I see full focus, full concentration. I see, 'OK, this is a problem, let's analyse it, and move on.'

"You see him in a debrief afterwards. You couldn't really say whether there was a bad or a good session. It's all very balanced and stable."

Antonelli took advice on this when he met tennis legend Roger Federer at Wimbledon this summer.

"We chatted about my races," Antonelli says. "About when he used to play, and about life in general.

"About pressure, he just told me to focus on one race at a time, just focus on what you can control, and also to control the emotions, especially the ones that can make you do mistakes."

Federer's words echoed something Marco has always impressed on his son.

"In our family, we use this concept in normal life as well," he says.

"We have to live every day our best day. You work hard every day to arrive at the end of the project you have."

Back in February 2024, Wolff followed up his phone call to Marco with a meeting in Milan.

"Toto said 'Of course it will be difficult, but I think after one year of experience, we can do very well with Kimi in F1'," Marco says.

"The project was 2025 experience, 2026 start to achieve results. I think we overachieved."

articles.title: Oficial: Carlos Sainz renueva con Williams
articles.standfirst: El español firma un acuerdo multianual con los de Grove que le mantendrá en la estructura británica en el futuro inminente
articles.summary: El español firma un acuerdo multianual con los de Grove que le mantendrá en la estructura británica en el futuro inminente
articles.body: Todo hacía indicar, como venía contando MARCA desde hace varios días, que Carlos Sainz sólo pensaba en Williams y que su renovación sería inminente después de semanas de reunión y reflexión en el parón estival, y la primera ficha en el tablero de los británicos al confirmar que su compañero, Alex Albon, también continuaría. No ha habido dudas, el madrileño seguirá con el azul de Grove en un acuerdo multianual, sin especificar el curso de finalización como se viene haciendo en los acuerdos de la Fórmula 1 moderna. Sainz es uno de los activos más valiosos de la Fórmula 1 y su papel seguirá pasando por liderar a Williams. Fue vital en el subidón de 2025, con dos cajones de Gran Premio y uno sprint que rompían una sequía para los británicos desde Bélgica 2021 (aquella carrera del diluvio donde Russell aprovechó su posición de salida al no competirse). En la segunda mitad de la campaña alcanzó un nivel altísimo, permitiendo que los británicos fuesen el quinto clasificado en la parrilla de forma holgada. En 2026 la situación es menos feliz, pero el madrileño vuelve a levantar la mano para tratar de enderezar el rumbo de una fábrica que no aterrizó comprendiendo del todo bien qué requería la nueva era de la clase reina. En su defensa, pocas lo han podido hacer del todo. El acuerdo supone que Carlos Sainz va a cobrar entorno a los 30 millones de euros, según ha podido saber MARCA, con lo que entraría en un nivel que sólo tienen ahora cinco pilotos en la F1: Verstappen, Hamilton Leclerc y Lando Norris. Un estatus de alguien que tiene el nivel de campeón del mundo o que lo sería con el coche adecuado. Los salarios más altos de la F1 Al respecto, habría que corregir que Sainz no estaba en 13 millones, como se deba por buenos en el 'paddock', sino bastante más arriba, más bien cerca de lo 20. Williams habría mejorado su sueldo en un tercio, que es muy destacable. Sainz ha firmado por dos años, aunque tiene cláusulas de posible salida al final de la primera, algo que no le gustaría tener que ejecutar, ya que sería la demostración de que el proyecto camina después del terrible inicio de 2026. Además, ha habido conversaciones con otros equipos, pero el español tenía claro que no quería bajarse del barco de Vowles y Williams a la primera, ya que se siente muy identificado con esta misión de devolver a los de Grove a la cabeza que un día ejercieron en la F1. “Creo en el trabajo de este equipo, tanto en el circuito como la fábrica y la inversión a largo plazo. Tenemos que dar la vuelta a esto juntos. Sigo tan comprometido como el primer día, tratando de devolver a lo que pertenecen, y quiero seguir creando recuerdos juntos”, defiende Sainz en el comunicado oficial. Fiel a su mensaje, de trabajo y capacidad de cambiar a los equipos como siempre ha demostrado desde que se subió a un Toro Rosso, pasó por Renault y desembarcó en dos grandes, McLaren y Ferrari. Allí dejó huella y hace no mucho tiempo seguía ese mensaje en la Scuderia en el que se extrañaba el trabajo metódico del español. Algo que ni Leclerc, muy explosivo pero menos analítico que Sainz, ni Hamilton, que ha necesitado un coche a su medida para volver a rendir, logran. Son condicionantes que valoran, lógicamente en la estructura británica, con un James Vowles que siempre ha admirado al piloto español. “Desde que llegó Carlos, su talento fue muy valioso trabajando para el proyecto. Es un líder, y estoy ansioso de ver qué logramos juntos y lo posible de reconstruir. Carlos comparte nuestra ambición y empuja todos los días para ello. Somos un equipo capaz de pelear por cada gramo de rendimiento”, admite. A ello se unirá un salario de piloto estrella, algo que también es un mensaje sobre la nueva realidad de los británicos, con capacidad de atraer a mejores pilotos y patrocinadores que apoyen a su proyecto. La renovación de Sainz se oficializa, como se vive en los tiempos modernos de la Fórmula 1, sin apuntar a la fecha concreta de finalización del concreto. Partirá del 2027, irá al 2028 y cuenta con la capacidad de ejecutar cláusulas de rendimiento si se presentan oportunidades lejos de Williams. En este mercado se le vinculó a Audi, pero no pasó de un mero rumor, pues el ‘55’ y su entorno se centraban totalmente en las conversaciones con Williams. Allí seguirá en el corto plazo, buscando más competitividad tras el sinsabor del 2026. Que es una realidad que Sainz no ha dudado en admitir mientras ponía deberes a su equipo. El primer golpe dramático llegó al aterrizar tarde el invierno, empezar con un coche muy pasado de peso y tener que remontar. A ello se sumó que las actualizaciones recientes no arrojaron todos los beneficios que esperaban desde el túnel de viento. Todo ello se suma y deja un panorama en el que Williams querrá dar un salto más en Bakú y el foco pasará a ser 2027 pese a que el FW48 todavía pueda recibir algún tipo de retoque. En todo ese trabajo, Sainz es clave. Volviendo a liderar a los de Grove, manteniendo una velocidad a una vuelta y en carrera que es superior a la de su compañero Albon y luchando por resultados pese a que tiene que sobreponerse a una máquina que no está, de momento, a la altura de las manos del español. Su futuro sigue pintándose de azul. El 55 seguirá luchando.

articles.title: Sainz, renovación galáctica: "Tenemos todos los ingredientes para devolver a Williams a lo más alto"
articles.standfirst: El español relata a los medios oficiales del equipo británico su compromiso fiel con la estructura de Grove
articles.summary: El español relata a los medios oficiales del equipo británico su compromiso fiel con la estructura de Grove
articles.body: La gran noticia justo antes del regreso al paddock de la Fórmula 1 con motivo del Gran Premio de los Países Bajos, en el majestuoso Zandvoort, es la renovación de Carlos Sainz en el equipo Williams. No tanto por el hecho en sí, que parecía lógico. Y sí por una apuesta a lo grande. Que tiene que ver con un sueldo galáctico (cercano a 30 millones por curso), en el top-5 de la parrilla. Y una apuesta total para que el madrileño sea el que devuelva a los británicos a la zona alta. Ya lo hicieron en 2025, pasando del fondo de la parrilla a ser la quinta fuerza del campeonato. Y el 2026 arrojará una situación parecida que Sainz afrontará. "El objetivo es el mismo: devolver al equipo a donde pertenece. Será un camino duro, pero tenemos los ingredientes correctos para lograrlo. Si nos focalizamos en el proceso, los detalles y creemos en el instinto, estoy convencido de que llegarán los resultados. Es el desafío y estoy listo para ello", defendió en los medios oficiales del equipo. Sainz será en Zandvoort un protagonista clave tras un proceso en el que valoró qué era lo mejor para su carrera y sus objetivos internos. La respuesta fue seguir. "Hay razones para hacerlo. La principal, por la gente que forma esta familia, y creo en esa fuerza para ser exitosos. Tenemos el talento, la motivación y la pasión para devolver al equipo a lo más alto. Además, hay cambios, inversiones y proyectos ocurriendo que me hacen creer que vamos en lo correcto", añadió. Sin obviar lo evidente. "Este curso fue un bache en el camino, pero tenemos los ingredientes correctos para lograr salir más fuertes", explicó. En esos ingredientes parece que existen dos caminos clave. Uno es el trabajo interno del equipo para encontrar qué falla y cómo solucionarlo. "Sigo lo que ocurre de forma interna, tanto en pista como en la fábrica y los cambios que veo son excitantes. Es cuestión de tiempo que todo funcione junto, y ver los resultados en pista", detalló. Y se une una materia gris prometedora que encabeza James Vowles. "Una cosa que valoro mucho es la relación directa. Lo vivo con todos, es importante ser honesto y transparente, con un ambiente donde se tome responsabilidad de las decisiones que tomamos. Es el tipo de conversación que tenemos en este equipo", lanzó. Su reto será volver a pelear por objetivos importantes, como los dos podios de Gran Premio y el de sprint del 2025. "El sentimiento que tuve cuando crucé la meta en Bakú [su primer cajón] no puedo explicarlo con palabras. Siempre lo recordaré. Y hay otras cosas que la gente no ve y son destacadas, como encontrar soluciones cuando pasas un fin de semana sufriendo viendo que tu sensaciones en el simulador y el trabajo ha funcionado. Te hace sentir orgulloso y te hace sentir empujando", recordó. Así las cosas, la carrera del 55 seguirá teñido de azul. "Veo a Williams como una gran familia y los fans son muy importantes. Nos dan la inspiración y fuerza para que podamos hacerles sentir orgullosos. Sus mensajes y cánticos nos ayudan, tanto a mí como a todo el equipo. Y cuando visten el azul nos elevan tras días duros", cerró. Sigue creyendo. "Tenemos un camino largo por delante, pero nada me haría más feliz que llegar juntos al destino", cerró.

articles.title: Item surprises big two for Juddmonte International glory
articles.summary: We were treated to another epic renewal of the Juddmonte International on Wednesday but it was far from the match-race that it was built up to be, with Item delivered late to deny Almaqam in a thrilling finish to the York feature.
articles.body:
Hawk Mountain rather unexpectedly set the early pace, with stablemate Constitution River tucked in keenly behind him and odds-on favourite Ombudsman at the rear under William Buick, kept company by another Aidan O'Brien runner, Action.

Hawk Mountain was still in front as they moved to the top of the long Knavesmire straight, with Buick beginning to make headway on the inside rail, as Ryan Moore and Constitution River kicked for home over two furlongs out.

Ombudsman kept making ground on the inside, but the dangers were coming on the outside and it was Ed Walker's Almaqam who pulled away with half a furlong to run, only for Item to arrive in full flight, just getting his head down on the line in the hands of Colin Keane.

Balding has now achieved something his later father, Ian, the trainer of Mill Reef, never managed. He said: "I don't think he had many goes at it, though, in fairness. It's always one of the most important races of the year. So it's lovely to win it with a horse like this.

"We've pitched him in some good races with the belief that he will do well in them, but he's kept improving and improved physically. That's the most important thing.

"He's really a very different horse than the one that ran in the Dante, physically."

He added: "I think anything is possible, he certainly has no problem staying a mile and a half if he wanted to.

"I just want to say a big thank you to the team at home because it wasn't straightforward getting him here. Everything had gone great up until about declaration time and we had a little hiccup there with his feet.

"Thankfully everyone who looks after him have worked overtime to get it right, and happily it was a 5am decision that he got on the box to come up here. I'm very relieved."

On Item's next assignment, the Kingsclere handler said: "I just do not know at this moment in time. I think we've got to sit down and let the dust settle. We've just won a Juddmonte International, that was the plan."

articles.title: Hollie Doyle: Kalpana can prove too hot for Yorkshire Oaks rivals
articles.summary: Kalpana is looking to back up her King George success in the Yorkshire Oaks on day two of York's Ebor Festival; Doyle believes Juddmonte Farms and Andrew Balding can make it two Group Ones in two days.
articles.body:
Kalpana too hot for Minnie in Yorkshire Oaks

Kalpana , a brilliant winner of the King George last month, will prove too hot for Minnie Hauk to handle in Thursday's showstopper at York, the Group One Legends Global Yorkshire Oaks (3.35).

The great French horse Calandagan simply had no answer to Andrew Balding's mare at Ascot, where Aidan O'Brien's multiple Oaks winner finished a disappointing 18 lengths adrift.

That was the second time in a row Minnie Hauk has put in an underwhelming performance and I just can't see her re-capturing her best form in time to bridge that yawning gap. Back against her own sex, Kalpana is simply irresistible, even if the forecast rain arrives.

At bigger odds, I hope to see David Menuisier's Inis Mor maintain the progress that has seen her make the frame in both the French and Irish Oaks. This is tougher still, but Oisin Murphy knows how to get the best out of her.

Irish filly ready to step into Pattern company

Juddmonte's Irish-trained filly Livenka looks ready to stamp her class on the Group Two Sky Bet Lowther Stakes (1.50) at York on Thursday.

Ger Lyons' daughter of Bated Breath booked her place in this line-up by taking a valuable sales race at Naas by nearly four lengths, suggesting she's ready to step into Pattern company.

She's drawn high but isn't far away from the probable favourite Libertango , the Albany winner who only narrowly lost her unbeaten record in the Group Two Duchess Of Cambridge at Newmarket.

George Boughey's filly sets the standard, but Livenka arrives on an upward curve and looks too smart to ignore, while Andrew Balding's Moonrise is another big player. She was second in the Windsor Castle at Royal Ascot before winning the Princess Margaret yet has been largely overlooked in the Ante-post markets.

My husband Tom (Marquand) and his boss William Haggas can expect a big run from Rhapsody in the British EBF & Sir Henry Cecil Galtres Stakes (4.10) at York - but she has one filly in particular to be fearful of.

Rhapsody brings ideal credentials to this Listed race with a Group placing and a course win to her name. However, I'm expecting Ralph Backett's A La Prochaine to take full advantage of this drop-in class.

Still lightly raced, she ran well in the Cheshire Oaks in the spring but stepped forward again to be fourth in the Oaks itself at Epsom on her latest start. She's been freshened up since then and looks a much sounder proposition than the likely favourite Morrophore , who's best form has been achieved on the All-Weather. She must also overcome an eight-month absence.

It's pretty unusual to see a Group One winner in a sales race but the participation of Sun Goddess in the Harry's Half Million By Goffs (2.25) at York demonstrates the limitless strength in depth at Ballydoyle.

Aidan O'Brien's Phoenix Stakes heroine looks thrown in on these terms and will probably go off an even shorter priced favourite if her Albany victor Libertango wins the Lowther.

Still, anything can happen in big-field sales races so there has to be some value in Clive Cox's unbeaten Satellite Of Love , who has over a stone to find with Sun Goddess but has a plum low draw and a progressive profile to go with it.

She really impressed me in her Newbury novice while I am also keeping an eye out for my boss Archie Watson's game filly Vollering , who has already picked up valuable black type in France and has plenty of experience now.

Bullet Point ready to follow up big Handicap

Bullet Point came back to form in timely fashion in this month's Shergar Cup and can go one better in the Sir Kevin Sinfield 7 In 7 Grand Finale Handicap (3.00) at York.

Last year's winner was clearly transformed by the first-time cheekpieces at Ascot and looks another winning chance for Tom (Marquand) if the headgear proves as effective a second time.

Ralph Beckett's Ante-post favourite Centigrade looks short enough for a horse stepping out of an All-Weather novice but I'd like to see Jack Channon's Mezcala involved at the business end of the race. The Buckingham Palace winner hasn't been blessed with the best of draws in stall 17 but will enjoy York if he gets that all-important luck in running.

Hollie Doyle was speaking to Sky Sports Racing's Simon Mapletoft .

articles.title: Kevin Blake's Ebor Festival tips: Sky Sports Racing expert looks ahead to day two at York with three selections
articles.summary: Day two of the York Ebor Festival takes place on Thursday and is headlined by the Yorkshire Oaks; Sky Sports Racing's Kevin Blake has put up three selections on the card on the Knavesmire
articles.body:
The Ebor Festival at York rolls on into day two on Thursday and while the main events will provide world-class action for us to enjoy, it is the supporting card that might well offer the best betting opportunities.

The Sir Kevin Sinfield 7 In 7 Grand Finale Handicap (3:00) is yet another brutally-tough handicap puzzle to solve, but William Haggas may have the answer in the shape of BULLET POINT . The five-year-old won this race last year off a mark of 100, enjoying a smooth trip around from a good draw and winning with some authority.

However, his career hasn't continued on the upward curve as might have been expected since then, with a trip down to Australia ending in disappointment followed by a six-month absence. Since his return, it wouldn't be at all surprising if his connections have been working backwards from this race.

He shaped with subtle promise in two runs in valuable handicaps earlier this season and then returned from another 12 weeks off to run a fine race in defeat at the Shergar Cup, finding just one that had got loose on the lead too good for him. He gets to run off the same mark of 101 here and while the draw hasn't been quite so good to him this year as it was last year, he still looks to have leading prospects.

The next contest of interest is the Mews Hotel Ossett EBF Stallions Nursery (4:45). Three weeks ago, this column put up the Hugo Palmer-trained MIA FANTASIA in a valuable nursery at Glorious Goodwood. To say he had a troubled passage would be underselling it! He got next to no luck in running and shaped much better than the bare result.

The case that made for him that day remains relevant, with him having overcome his inexperience to win in good style at Carlisle on debut before not quite being sharp enough to be as competitive in what has proven to be a smart novice contest at Ascot that was won by the subsequent Vintage Stakes winner Dr Rascal. A mark of 79 seems very fair indeed and he is sure to have benefited from the experience he gained at Goodwood. He looks likely to run a big race.

The final race of interest on the day is another very tough handicap, the British EBF Fillies' Handicap (5:20). Again, cases can be made for so many of these, but I'm going to venture down towards the bottom end of the weights and side with the Ed Walker-trained SECRET HISTORY .

The three-year-old has already won three times this year, with her most notable victory coming in a valuable seven-furlong handicap at Newmarket in July. Raised 4lb for that, her connections took a chance in dropping her to six furlongs to contest a valuable fillies' handicap at Glorious Goodwood and while she ran well to finish third, she shaped as though the test was sharper than ideal for her. Returning to this trip will be a big help to her and she looks to have very strong prospects.

articles.title: Sainz renueva... ¿y Alonso?
articles.standfirst: El español de Williams se aseguró uno de los mejores contratos de la parrilla y el foco del futuro pasa a su compatriota que todavía no ha comunicado su decisión
articles.summary: El español de Williams se aseguró uno de los mejores contratos de la parrilla y el foco del futuro pasa a su compatriota que todavía no ha comunicado su decisión
articles.body: la primera ficha en el tablero de los españoles en la Fórmula 1 cayó con la renovación a lo grande de Carlos Sainz por Williams. Su nuevo contrato, de unos 30 millones por temporada, le dispara a los guarismos de otras estrellas de la parrilla, como el último campeón Lando Norris. Y deja al otro piloto que compite con la rojigualda en el casco, Fernando Alonso, con los focos colocados encima de su gran decisión. La de alargar una carrera deportiva que viene desde 2001 batallando en la élite y tiene las dos coronas (2005 y 2006) como joyas. Si bien es cierto que existieron voces que mezclaron su futuro en la parrilla, esas posibilidades no pasarán de rumores con un Sainz que no dudó de su continuidad en Williams tras semanas de debate con su entorno y el propio equipo británico. "Tenemos todos los ingredientes para volver a lo más alto", defendió tras estampar su firma en su nuevo contrato multianual. Por su parte, Fernando Alonso vive una situación similar, pues Aston Martin será la firma que acompañe su decisión. Esté en pista en el proyecto con Newey y Honda o decida dar un paso al costado. "Yo tengo contrato, sigo", contó. Los dos españoles son los líderes claros de sus proyectos deportivos y también se han encontrado con una parrilla que apenas mueve fichas o apuesta por otros nombres. Quizá el papel de animador de la silly-season corresponde a Alpine y Gucci -estructura vinculada a varios nombres de prestigio-, pero no es una escudería llamada a asaltar la zona alta. En Mercedes, Ferrari, McLaren y Red Bull, las cuatro dominadoras de la parrilla, los movimientos se antojan imposibles. Aunque Verstappen y su entorno agitan el avispero, los movimientos apuntan más a 2028 con nuevos contratos que volver a negociar. Así las cosas, por Alonso y Sainz pasará la reacción de sus equipos para llegar a la zona alta. En Williams existe fe en el proceso, mientras que Aston Martin formó un equipo de élite a velocidad de vértigo, pero se encontró con un inicio de 2026 para olvidar. Eso sí, no tiene que ver con la decisión de Alonso, que apunta a otros factores como el conjunto de normas de la F1. Pero es el mismo tablero para todos. "El reglamento es lo que los equipos o la federación piensan que es mejor; así que hay que sacar partido al coche para ganar carreras, estar arriba y pensar en el próximo reglamento cuando venga. Ahora es lo que tenemos y hay que hacerlo mejor", reconoció en las últimas carreras antes del verano. Eso sí, con el anuncio de Sainz queda su decisión como último gran punto culminante, más allá del rumbo final de Verstappen. En este 2026 no ha terminado de aclarar qué pasa por su cabeza. Sí pasó por una despedida adelantada en Montmeló, otros mensajes que parecían camino de la continuidad, y desemboca en un debate que todavía no tiene respuesta. O por lo menos, de cara al exterior. Quizá en Holanda arroje luz a su corto plazo en la F1.
